title: Convoys at the Finish
statement:
Cars drive in the same direction along a one-lane road toward a finish line at mile target. Car i starts at mile position[i] and drives at speed[i] miles per hour.

A car can never pass the car in front of it. When a faster car catches up with a slower one, it slows down and the two drive on together as one convoy, at the speed of the slower car. Several cars can end up in one convoy. A car that catches another car exactly at the finish line also counts as part of its convoy. A single car alone is a convoy too.

Return how many convoys cross the finish line.

examples.why: The car at 14 needs 3 hours, as does the car at 17, so they meet exactly at the finish: one convoy. The car at 2 needs only 6 hours on its own, but it gets stuck behind the slow car at 9 (11 hours): the second convoy.
The back car is faster, yet it needs 4.5 hours and the front car arrives after 4. Being faster is not enough; it must catch up before the finish.

Arrival times alone would be 10, 5 and 6 hours. The car at 70 is slower than the car right in front of it, but that car is already held back to 10 hours by the leader, so all three arrive together. Compare against the convoy's arrival time, not the previous car's.

hints: Cars can only be held up by cars in front of them. In which order should you look at the cars?
Work out each car's arrival time if it were alone: (target − position) / speed. Go from the car closest to the finish backwards. When does a car join the convoy in front of it?

A car joins the convoy ahead if its own time is at most that convoy's arrival time; otherwise it starts a new, slower convoy. Keep the arrival times of the convoys (a stack, or just the last one) and count them.

explain.intuition:
A car's fate depends only on the cars ahead of it, so sort by position and go from the front of the road to the back. Compute each car's solo arrival time. If a car would arrive no later than the convoy right in front of it, it catches that convoy before or at the finish and joins it, arriving at the convoy's time. If it would arrive later, it never catches anyone: it leads a new convoy.

The convoys' arrival times, from front to back, only ever increase. That is a monotonic stack; and since you only compare with the newest convoy, keeping its time in one variable is enough.
steps: Pair each car's position with its speed and sort by position, largest first.
For each car, compute time = (target − position) / speed.
If time is greater than the arrival time of the newest convoy, this car starts a new convoy: count it and remember its time.
Otherwise it merges into that convoy; the convoy's time does not change.
pitfalls: Comparing each car with the car directly in front of it instead of with that car's convoy. The leader's slowness is what holds the whole group.
Using < instead of <= for merging: a car that catches up exactly at the finish line joins the convoy.
Forgetting to sort. The input positions are in any order.

solutions.title: Check every car against all cars ahead
solutions.idea: A car leads its own convoy exactly when every car in front of it arrives strictly earlier on its own. Compare arrival times by cross-multiplying, so there is no rounding.

solutions.title: Sort, then a stack of convoy arrival times
solutions.idea: Go from the front car backwards. Push a car's arrival time only when it is later than the time on top; otherwise the car merges into the top convoy.

solutions.title: Sort, then track only the last convoy
solutions.idea: Only the newest convoy's time is ever compared, so the stack can shrink to one variable.

followups: Return, for each car, the time at which it first catches up with the car ahead, or -1 if it never does. Why does a plain stack no longer suffice?
Floating-point times could in principle compare equal when they should not. How would you compare two arrival times exactly?
